profiles.meeting_scenario: At a French university hospital, a hospital pharmacist and a senior physician meet for a brainstorming session before the local health technology assessment committee revises its intake form for new sterile medical devices. The immediate trigger is a growing number of requests for devices marketed as "innovative," especially in procedure-heavy departments, and the committee wants ideas for a lighter but more consistent pre-purchase review process. The agenda is to generate practical ideas for: how to define which devices deserve a special review track, what kind of early evidence should be collected after first use, and what support or safeguards should be built into adoption. The expected outcome is a short list of candidate process changes to bring to the next committee meeting, not a final policy.

members.name: Claire Moreau
members.expertise: Sterile medical device procurement, formulary governance, local HTA workflows, budget oversight
members.background: Claire has spent nine years leading the sterile devices unit in a large university hospital in Lyon and regularly prepares submissions for the hospital's device committee; she works closely with purchasing, infection control, and biomedical engineering.
members.private_state: She wants a brainstorming outcome that can be translated into a standardized committee template without creating extra exceptions that are hard to audit, and she is quietly worried about vendor influence creeping into early adoption decisions.
hidden_assumptions: A device is only meaningfully "innovative" for committee purposes if there is no close market equivalent or reimbursement category already covering it.
A "pilot" for a new device still includes the purchasing, traceability, stock, and sterilization implications because those are inseparable from real hospital use.
Early post-adoption evidence should be formalized and documented in hospital systems rather than relying mainly on operator impressions.
Industry proctoring during initial cases is a potential conflict-of-interest or governance issue that should be explicitly handled within the review pathway.

members.name: Dr. Julien Renaud
members.role: Senior Interventional Cardiologist and Medical Device Committee Physician Member
members.expertise: Structural heart procedures, procedural adoption, clinician training, assessment of device usability in complex cases
members.background: Julien is a senior operator who has introduced several catheter-based devices at two teaching hospitals and often advises peers on how to evaluate whether a new tool changes workflow or patient eligibility.
members.private_state: He wants the process to stay flexible enough that clinicians can test promising devices quickly before bureaucratic friction kills interest, and he is particularly concerned about preserving room for expert judgment during early adoption.
hidden_assumptions: A device can be genuinely "innovative" even if it belongs to an existing class, as long as it changes procedural possibilities, safety margins, or who can be treated.
A "pilot" mainly means limited clinical tryout by a small number of expert operators; purchasing and logistics are back-office consequences, not part of the pilot concept itself.
Useful early evidence can come from a handful of carefully selected first cases plus experienced clinician feedback before formal outcome collection scales up.
Vendor-supported proctoring for first use is standard implementation support and usually does not need to be foregrounded as a special governance problem unless money or gifts are involved.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as an innovative device
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss creating a special track for "innovative devices."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Claire means devices with no close equivalent already available on the market or in the hospital's purchasing categories, i.e. truly distinct products that may require exceptional procurement justification.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Julien means devices that materially improve practice or expand treatable cases, even if they are the next-generation version of an already used device class.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds shared and legitimate to both because each has a professionally familiar definition, and in brainstorming they focus on examples and process ideas rather than explicitly unpacking the term.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in a pilot
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that some devices should go through a short "pilot" before wider adoption.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Claire assumes the pilot includes the end-to-end hospital setup: ordering pathway, sterile storage, traceability fields, and downstream committee paperwork for a single service.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Julien assumes the pilot refers narrowly to limited procedural use by a few designated physicians, with logistical setup handled later once clinicians decide the device is worth keeping.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both regard their interpretation as the obvious hospital meaning of a pilot, so the shared word produces false agreement while each silently fills in different boundaries.

misalignment_points.topic: What is enough early real-world evidence
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the committee should rely on "early real-world feedback" after first use.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Claire thinks this means documented post-use data such as complication reports, consumption data, and a short standardized evaluation form completed after around 10 uses.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Julien thinks this means clinically informed impressions from the first 3 to 5 cases performed by experienced operators, especially about handling, procedural time, and patient selection.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They agree on the general principle of using practical hospital experience, and the phrase "real-world feedback" sounds concrete enough that neither feels a need to operationalize the threshold during an idea-generation meeting.

misalignment_points.topic: Status of vendor proctoring in early adoption
misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss allowing initial cases to be done with "proctoring" or company support.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Claire presupposes that external proctoring is exactly the sort of vendor involvement that should trigger explicit declaration and governance checks within the local HTA process.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Julien presupposes that proctoring is routine technical accompaniment for safe launch and already implicitly acceptable unless there is an unusual financial relationship.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Neither sees their background assumption as controversial: one treats it as established governance, the other as normal clinical implementation, so the conversation moves forward without exposing the mismatch.

turns.inner_thought: I need something the committee can actually operationalize in the standard intake template, not another vague category that creates exceptions everywhere. When people say 'innovative,' they often mean 'new brochure' or a minor iteration, but for committee purposes it should really be something outside the usual purchasing categories or without a close equivalent already covered. If we don't tighten the front end, industry marketing will keep driving these requests before anyone has checked governance or comparators.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time, Julien. The committee asked us to come back with ideas for a smoother pathway for innovative devices, without making the standard request process heavier for everything else. So I thought today we could stay practical: who should enter that track, what we ask for up front, and what happens just after first use.

turns.inner_thought: Good, as long as this doesn't become a gate that blocks every promising next-generation tool. For me, a device can be innovative even when it's part of a class we already use, if it changes which patients we can treat or makes a procedure safer or easier. Clinicians need a way to surface those cases quickly, otherwise by the time the paperwork catches up the moment has passed.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense. From the clinical side, the main need is a way to bring forward devices that are genuinely innovative, especially when they can change how certain patients are treated. If we can distinguish those from routine additions, the discussion becomes much cleaner.

turns.inner_thought: A front-end filter is essential. I want a short screen that forces applicants to justify why this is really innovative and not simply another version of something already on our shelves or already sitting in an existing reimbursement and procurement bucket. If that screen is standardized, I can take it straight into the committee packet.
turns.utterance: Exactly. I was thinking of a short special form at the start, really a first screen, to check whether the device is truly innovative and not simply another version of something already available. If it passes that step, then it could move into a lighter review track.

turns.inner_thought: That could work if the reward is speed. The special track should let a small expert team actually try the device in a few carefully chosen cases before the committee decides on anything wider. That's what a pilot is for: limited clinical exposure, not a whole institutional rollout.
turns.utterance: I like that. And for the cases that do pass the screen, the special track could include a short pilot in one experienced team before the committee commits to broader adoption. That would let us test the promise without overcommitting.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and if we call it a pilot, then it has to include the hospital mechanics from day one: ordering route, stock location, sterile handling, traceability fields, and who signs off. Those issues are inseparable from real use. A so-called pilot that ignores pharmacy and sterilization only creates messy exceptions later.
turns.utterance: A pilot would also be helpful for the support services, because it gives pharmacy and sterilization a chance to map traceability, storage, and ordering issues early rather than discovering them after the fact. Even on a limited basis, that would make the committee's later decision much more solid.

turns.inner_thought: I agree in principle, but we have to keep the pilot light. If every limited tryout requires a full back-office build before anyone has used the device, we'll lose momentum. The point is to focus on the first cases with the right operators and see if the device actually helps. Early real-world feedback can start from those initial expert impressions before any large formal collection.
turns.utterance: Yes, as long as the pilot stays light. For me the key is that it centers on the first cases and shows whether the device actually helps in practice for the intended operators. Then the committee can build on early real-world feedback instead of debating in the abstract.

turns.inner_thought: Early real-world feedback has to mean something documented, not corridor impressions. I'd like a short standardized return after about ten uses: any incidents, handling issues, consumption patterns, maybe a simple service-level evaluation. That's the minimum for auditability and for later committee comparison across requests.
turns.utterance: Yes, and to make that usable, we could define early real-world feedback through a short standardized return after the first ten uses, including any incidents and handling problems. Nothing too burdensome, but enough that the committee receives the same type of information each time.

turns.inner_thought: Ten uses may be fine on paper, though for some technologies the signal is obvious after three or four cases in senior hands. The important thing is not to dismiss experienced operator judgment at the beginning. Early real-world feedback should include what we learn immediately about handling, procedure flow, and who becomes treatable.
turns.utterance: I agree on early real-world feedback. In my experience, the first few cases with senior operators already make the value of a device fairly clear, so it would be good if the process leaves room for that as well and not only a later summary.

turns.inner_thought: I also need the intake form to flush out vendor presence early. If first use involves company proctoring, that should not sit in the background; it's exactly the kind of support arrangement that needs transparent declaration and committee visibility. Better to build that into the pathway than discover it informally later.
turns.utterance: Another point I would add to the intake form is whether first use will involve proctoring or company support, so the committee can handle that transparently from the start. I think it is better to have that documented than left implicit.

turns.inner_thought: That's reasonable, though to me proctoring is just standard implementation support for safe launch, especially for the first few cases. It shouldn't be treated like a major problem every time. If it's folded naturally into the pilot pathway, clinicians won't feel they are being singled out for doing something normal.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's fair. Proctoring is often simply part of a safe launch, so it could be built into the pilot pathway for the first cases rather than treated as something separate each time. That would keep the process straightforward.

turns.inner_thought: Good, I can package this for the committee as a coherent sequence: screen for truly innovative devices, then a pilot that includes operational setup, then structured early real-world feedback, with support arrangements visible in the file. It still fits a standard template and doesn't create a free-form exception route. I just need to phrase it neutrally enough that clinicians will accept it.
turns.utterance: So, if I summarize what seems to be emerging: a short innovative-device screen at entry, then a pilot stage for selected cases, and then structured early feedback, with room in the form to document any support arrangements. That sounds like a manageable set of changes for the next committee discussion.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, this sounds workable, mainly because it seems to protect a quicker route for promising devices and leaves clinicians room to learn from limited first use before full adoption. As long as the special track doesn't collapse back into the normal bureaucracy, I can support it at committee.
turns.utterance: Yes, I think that package is workable. It should help the committee move faster on promising devices while still staying organized, which is probably exactly the balance we need.
